welcome.title: Welcome to Campus Companion
welcome.body: Your first weeks at university can feel like a lot, and that is completely normal. This app puts what you need in one place. Take a one-minute tour. You cannot get anything wrong.
welcome.hint: Skip any time. You can replay this tour from your Profile.

home.title: Your home base
home.body: Home shows the latest announcements, shuttle times for your stop, and quick links to everything else. A NEW tag means an announcement went out recently and you have not opened it yet.
home.hint: Scroll down on Home for Sport & gym, programmes and FAQs.

search.title: Find anything, fast
search.body: Not sure where to look? Use the search bar. It searches answers, venues, sessions, people to contact and guides, all at once.
search.hint: Look for the search bar at the top of Home.

schedule.title: Know where to be, and when
schedule.body: See your orientation sessions with their times and venues. Switch to Campus events to see what is on around campus.

map.title: Never get lost
map.body: The campus map shows buildings and venues. Find a place and get walking directions to it.

checklist.title: Tick off the essentials
checklist.body: The new student checklist lists what to sort out in your first weeks, like registration and your student email. Go at your own pace and tick things off as you finish them.
checklist.hint: Find it on Home: New student checklist.

digital.title: Get digital-ready
digital.body: Step-by-step guides for Funda, Wi-Fi and printing, plus short lessons on file management, staying safe online, strong passwords and using AI tools responsibly.

tribe.title: Meet your Tribe
tribe.body: Your Tribe is a chat with your mentor and other first-years. Before you choose a chat name you will agree to keep it respectful. Tap Find groups to browse mentor groups or scan a QR code.

help.title: Help is always close
help.body: Not sure who to ask? Open Support, choose what you need help with, and the app points you to the right person or service. Contacts lists mentors and advisors you can reach directly. For urgent help, use the red Emergency contacts card on Home.

profile.title: Make it yours
profile.body: In Profile you can switch between English, isiXhosa and Afrikaans, choose light or dark mode, and make the text bigger. You can replay this tour there whenever you like.

shuttle.chooseHint: Choose your stop to see when your shuttle leaves.
shuttle.chooseAbove: Choose your stop above and your times will appear here.

boarding-requirement.title: Boarding requirement
boarding-requirement.text: To board the shuttle, all students must present a valid student ID card along with their proof of acceptance or registration letter.

early-arrival.title: Early arrival
early-arrival.text: Students wishing to arrive early on campus are advised to take the first scheduled shuttle of the day.

assistance.title: Assistance
assistance.text: Shuttle marshals are available to assist. Students who are unsure of the correct shuttle should ask a marshal for guidance.

code-of-conduct.title: Code of conduct
code-of-conduct.text: Students are required to follow marshal and driver instructions at all times. Disrespectful behaviour or refusal to comply will result in immediate suspension of shuttle service privileges.

prohibited-items-and-behaviour.title: Prohibited items and behaviour
prohibited-items-and-behaviour.text: No eating or drinking is permitted inside the shuttles. Alcohol is strictly prohibited. Any student deemed to be intoxicated will be denied access.

conduct.title: Before you join the conversation
conduct.intro: Tribe is part of Nelson Mandela University's public communication platforms. What you write here represents you and the University, so we keep it respectful and safe for everyone.
conduct.respect: I will treat everyone in Tribe with respect: my mentor, the coordinators and every other student.
conduct.bully: I will not bully, harass, threaten, shame or exclude anyone.
conduct.swear: I will not swear or use offensive, hateful or discriminatory language.
conduct.private: I will keep my own private details, and other people's, private.
conduct.watched: I understand that mentors and coordinators can read Tribe messages, and that messages that break these rules can be removed.
conduct.agree: I have read this and I agree to follow it.

buddy.heroText: You are the friendly face that makes a first-year feel they belong. You do not need to know everything. You just need to know where to point.
buddy.banner: Many new students ask the questions they think are obvious. Treat every question as a good one.

courage.title: Courage
courage.text: Encourage the next small step: attend the session, ask the question, send the email.

empathy.title: Empathy
empathy.text: Orientation can feel overwhelming. Use warm, plain words and skip the jargon.

vulnerability.title: Vulnerability
vulnerability.text: Make it safe to say "I do not know yet". Share a time you felt the same.

shame.title: Shame resilience
shame.text: Never make anyone feel late, lost or foolish. Always leave them with a next step.

boundaries.b1: You are a buddy, not a counsellor. For serious worries about safety or wellbeing, refer the student to professional support and tell the orientation coordinators.
boundaries.b2: Never ask for ID numbers, medical details or financial information, and do not share what a student tells you in confidence.
boundaries.b3: Keep Tribe chats respectful. Orientation staff can read them to help keep the space safe.
boundaries.b4: If you do not know the answer, say so, then find it together in the Answers tab or ask a coordinator.

checklist.c3: Look at this week's schedule and know where the venues are
checklist.c4: Save the key contacts in the Refer tab

soc.whatIs: A society is a student-run club you can join for the year. Some are built around a faith, some around what you study, and some around a cause or a skill that has nothing to do with your degree. You pay a small once-off fee, and in return you get people who already know what you are going through. You do not need to be good at anything, know anyone, or commit to every meeting — turning up once is enough to start.

about.label: ABOUT THE PROJECT
about.subtitle: School of IT Student Orientation App
about.summary: Built to help first-year School of IT students feel welcome, informed and ready. It brings the orientation schedule, venues, contacts, FAQs, support and digital skills guides into one place, so nobody has to piece it together from emails and messages.
about.status: This is a hackathon prototype. Content shown may be sample data until staff publish the real orientation programme.

principles.courage: Clear next steps and small wins, so taking the first step feels doable.
principles.empathy: Warm, plain language. We never assume you already know how university works.
principles.vulnerability: Not knowing something yet is normal. The guides and FAQs are here for exactly that.
principles.shame: Missed a session or feeling lost? You will always be shown what to do next, never blamed.

features.f1: Home with announcements, shuttle times and your progress
features.f2: Search across the schedule, FAQs, contacts, venues and help options
features.f4: Campus map for South and North campus: building numbers, search, walking routes
features.f6: Digital readiness guides: computer skills, Funda, printing and Wi-Fi
features.f8: Support pathways ("I need help with...") and key contacts
features.f9: Tribe: a chat with the students in your mentor group
features.f10: Language switcher (English, isiXhosa, Afrikaans), dark mode and adjustable text size
features.f11: Saved copy of key information for when your connection drops

keep.label: What we keep
keep.text: Your email address (to sign you in), the chat name you choose for Tribe, the messages you send there, and which digital readiness steps you have finished.

never.label: What we never ask for
never.text: ID numbers, medical details or financial information.

who.label: Who can see it
who.text: Tribe messages are visible to the students in your tribe and to orientation staff, who help keep the space safe. Your progress is only yours.

device.label: On your device
device.text: Your language, text size and theme, your last few searches, plus a saved copy of the schedule, FAQs and contacts so they work offline.

map.label: The campus map
map.text: The map loads its pictures and walking routes from free OpenStreetMap-based services. They only receive which part of the map you are viewing and the start and end points of a route. The app does not use GPS and never tracks where you are. Your name and account are never sent.

approach.label: Our approach
approach.text: Designed with POPIA principles in mind: collect only what is needed, and keep private details private.

about.helpText: This app points you towards help. It does not replace it. If you are struggling, or you or someone else may be in danger, contact the university counselling and wellness services or campus protection services straight away. Asking for help early is a smart, responsible thing to do.

file-management.title: Basic file management
file-management.subtitle: New to files and folders? Work through these short lessons in order.

files-1-files-and-folders.title: Files and folders
files-1-files-and-folders.summary: What they are and how to open, browse and create them.
files-1-files-and-folders.desc: A file is one piece of work, like an essay or a photo. A folder holds files together, the way a paper folder holds pages.

steps.0: On a Windows computer, press the Windows key and E together to open File Explorer. On a phone, open the Files app.
steps.1: Look at the list on the left. Documents, Downloads and Desktop are places where your files can live.
steps.2: Double-click a folder to open it. Click the back arrow at the top to go up one level.
steps.3: To make your own folder, right-click an empty space, choose New, then Folder.
steps.4: Type a name for the folder and press Enter. Your folder is ready to use.

files-1-files-and-folders.tip: Most things you download end up in Downloads. Move the ones you want to keep into your own folders.

files-2-naming-and-organising.title: Naming and organising
files-2-naming-and-organising.summary: A simple folder plan so you can find your work fast.
files-2-naming-and-organising.desc: Clear names and a simple folder plan mean you can find your work in seconds, even the night before a deadline.

steps.0: Make one main folder for the year, for example '2027 First Year'.
steps.1: Inside it, make one folder for each module, such as 'Programming' or 'Networks'.
steps.2: Inside each module folder, add 'Assignments', 'Notes' and 'Study material'.
steps.3: Give files names that explain themselves, like 'Programming - Assignment 1 - Draft.docx'.
steps.4: Avoid names like 'final', 'final2' or 'new'. Add a date or a version number instead, like 'v2'.
steps.5: To rename a file, click it once, press F2, type the new name and press Enter.

files-2-naming-and-organising.tip: Windows does not allow these characters in a file name: / \ : * ? " < > |

files-3-save-copy-move.title: Saving, copying and moving
files-3-save-copy-move.summary: Keep your work, make a second version, or put it somewhere else.
files-3-save-copy-move.desc: Saving keeps your work. Copying makes a second version. Moving puts the original in a different place.

steps.0: Save as you work. In most programs, press Ctrl and S together, and do it every few minutes.
steps.1: The first time you save, choose the folder and type a clear name. Use Save As to keep another version under a new name.
steps.2: To copy a file, click it, press Ctrl and C, open the folder you want, then press Ctrl and V.
steps.3: To move a file, click it, press Ctrl and X, open the folder you want, then press Ctrl and V.
steps.4: You can also drag a file into a folder to move it. Hold Ctrl while you drag to copy it instead.

files-3-save-copy-move.tip: A cut file stays where it is until you paste it, so nothing is lost if you get interrupted halfway.

files-4-find-and-recover.title: Finding and recovering files
files-4-find-and-recover.summary: Search for a file, and get back one you deleted by mistake.
files-4-find-and-recover.desc: Everyone loses a file at some point. These steps help you find it again, or bring it back.

steps.0: In File Explorer, click the search box at the top right and type part of the file name.
steps.1: Open 'Quick access' (called 'Home' in Windows 11) to see the files you opened recently.
steps.2: Click the 'Date modified' heading to put your newest work at the top of a folder.
steps.3: If you deleted a file by mistake, open the Recycle Bin on your desktop.
steps.4: Right-click the file and choose Restore. It goes back to the folder it came from.

files-4-find-and-recover.tip: Once you empty the Recycle Bin, files are very hard to get back. Look through it before you empty it.

files-5-back-up.title: Backing up your work
files-5-back-up.summary: Keep every assignment in at least two places.
files-5-back-up.desc: Laptops get lost, broken and stolen. Keep your assignments in at least two places, so one problem never costs you your work.

steps.0: Sign in to OneDrive with your university email address. Your files copy to the cloud whenever you are online.
steps.1: Save your assignments in your OneDrive folder, or drag your module folders into it.
steps.2: Wait for the green tick on a file. It means the file has finished copying to the cloud.
steps.3: Keep a second copy on a USB drive for big deadlines.
steps.4: Back up before you submit, and before you update or reset your computer.

files-5-back-up.tip: Lab computers are shared. Save to OneDrive or a USB drive, and do not leave the only copy on the computer.

files-6-types-and-sharing.title: File types and sharing
files-6-types-and-sharing.summary: What .docx and .pdf mean, and how to send files safely.
files-6-types-and-sharing.desc: The letters after the dot in a file name show what kind of file it is and which program opens it.

steps.0: .docx is a Word document, .xlsx is an Excel sheet, .pptx is a PowerPoint and .pdf looks the same on every device.
steps.1: To see these letters, open the View tab in File Explorer and tick 'File name extensions'.
steps.2: Submit the type of file your lecturer asks for. For a PDF, choose File, then Save As or Export, and pick PDF.
steps.3: To send several files at once, select them, right-click, choose 'Compress to ZIP file' and attach the ZIP.
steps.4: For large files, share a OneDrive link instead of attaching the file to an email.
steps.5: Only open attachments from people you know. Unknown .exe and .zip files can carry viruses.

files-6-types-and-sharing.tip: Check the name of the file before you submit it. A lecturer marks what you upload, so make sure it is the latest version.

cyber-safety.title: Cyber safety
cyber-safety.subtitle: Spot scams, browse safely, and protect your device and your privacy.

safety-1-scams.title: Spotting scams and phishing
safety-1-scams.summary: Fake emails and messages that try to trick you.
safety-1-scams.desc: Phishing is a fake email, SMS or WhatsApp message that pretends to be someone you trust, like the university, a bank or a bursary. It tries to steal your details or your money.

steps.0: Slow down when a message feels urgent. Scammers say things like 'act now' or 'your account will be closed'.
steps.1: Check who really sent it. Look at the full email address, not just the name shown.
steps.2: Do not tap a link you did not expect. Type the website address yourself instead.
steps.3: Never share a password, PIN, one-time code or student number in reply to a message. Real organisations do not ask for these.
steps.4: Be suspicious of offers that sound too good to be true, like free data, easy jobs or a bursary you never applied for.
steps.5: If you are unsure, do not reply. Forward the message to IT Services and delete it.

safety-1-scams.tip: Check with the sender using a phone number or website you already trust, never one taken from the message.

safety-2-browsing.title: Safe browsing and public Wi-Fi
safety-2-browsing.summary: Habits that keep you safe on websites and networks.
safety-2-browsing.desc: Almost everything you do online goes through a website or a Wi-Fi network. A few habits keep you safe on both.

steps.0: Look for the padlock and https at the start of a website address before you enter personal details.
steps.1: Download apps only from the Play Store or App Store, and programs only from the official website.
steps.2: Be careful on free public Wi-Fi. Do not bank or enter passwords on a network you do not trust.
steps.3: On campus, connect to the official eduroam network, not an open network with a similar name.
steps.4: Log out of shared and lab computers when you finish, and close the browser.
steps.5: Do not tick 'remember me' or 'save password' on a shared computer.

safety-2-browsing.tip: A padlock only means the connection is private. It does not prove the website is honest, so still check the address.

safety-3-device.title: Protecting your device
safety-3-device.summary: Keep your phone and laptop safe, and your work with them.
safety-3-device.desc: Your phone and laptop hold your assignments, photos and accounts. Protect them the way you would protect your wallet.

steps.0: Lock your phone and laptop with a PIN, password, fingerprint or face unlock.
steps.1: Install updates when they appear. Updates fix security holes that criminals use.
steps.2: Keep antivirus switched on. Windows Security does this for free on a Windows computer.
steps.3: Do not leave your laptop or phone alone in the library, a lab or a taxi.
steps.4: Turn on Find My Device on Android, or Find My iPhone, so you can locate or wipe a lost phone.
steps.5: Back up your work, so a lost or infected device does not cost you an assignment.

safety-3-device.tip: Write down your laptop serial number and keep it somewhere safe. It helps if you ever need to report a theft.

safety-4-privacy.title: Privacy, social media and getting help
safety-4-privacy.summary: Think before you share, and know what to do if things go wrong.
safety-4-privacy.desc: What you post can stay online for years. Think before you share, and know what to do if something goes wrong.

steps.0: Think before you post. Anything you share can be copied, even if you delete it later.
steps.1: Keep your student number, ID number, address and timetable private.
steps.2: Use privacy settings so only people you know can see your posts and photos.
steps.3: Never share private photos of yourself or of other people without permission.
steps.4: If someone bullies or threatens you online, do not reply. Take screenshots, block them and tell someone you trust.
steps.5: If your account is hacked or you fell for a scam, change your password straight away and contact IT Services.

safety-4-privacy.tip: Being bullied online is never your fault. The Support section of this app can point you to people who can help.

password-safety.title: Password safety
password-safety.subtitle: Make a strong password, keep it safe and add extra protection.

password-1-strong.title: Building a strong password
password-1-strong.desc: The longer and more unusual a password is, the harder it is to guess. Length matters more than clever symbols.

steps.0: Aim for at least 12 characters. Longer is better.
steps.1: Use a passphrase: four or more random words, like 'purple-bicycle-river-toast'.
steps.2: Add numbers or symbols if you like, but do not rely on them to make a short password strong.
steps.3: Do not use your name, birthday, student number, cellphone number or 'password123'.
steps.4: Avoid common patterns such as 123456, qwerty or the name of your favourite team.

password-1-strong.tip: A long phrase that only means something to you is easier to remember and harder to crack than a short jumble like P@ssw0rd.

password-2-keep-safe.title: Keeping your passwords safe
password-2-keep-safe.summary: One password per account, and never share it.
password-2-keep-safe.desc: A strong password only helps if nobody else gets it. Keep each one private, and different.

steps.0: Use a different password for every important account, especially your student email and your banking.
steps.1: Never share a password with a friend, a lecturer or anyone who messages you. Nobody real needs it.
steps.2: Use a password manager to remember them for you. Your phone or browser may already have one built in.
steps.3: Do not keep passwords on sticky notes, or in a plain file called 'passwords' on your computer.
steps.4: Never type a password after tapping a link in a message. Go to the website yourself.

password-2-keep-safe.tip: If one site is hacked and you used the same password everywhere, criminals will try it on all your other accounts.

password-3-two-step.title: Extra protection, and what to do if it leaks
password-3-two-step.summary: Two-step checks and quick action after a leak.
password-3-two-step.desc: Two-step verification adds a second check, so a stolen password on its own is not enough to get into your account.

steps.0: Turn on two-step verification, also called multi-factor authentication, for your email and other important accounts.
steps.1: Use an authenticator app or a code sent to your phone as the second step.
steps.2: Keep your backup codes somewhere safe, in case you lose your phone.
steps.3: If you think a password has leaked, change it straight away, then change it anywhere else you used it.
steps.4: You can check whether your email address appeared in a known data breach at haveibeenpwned.com.
steps.5: If you cannot log in to a university account, contact IT Services to reset it.

password-3-two-step.tip: Never give a verification code to anyone, even someone who says they are from the university or your bank.

responsible-ai.title: Responsible use of AI tools
responsible-ai.subtitle: Use AI to learn, check what it tells you, and stay honest in your work.

ai-1-what-it-is.title: What AI tools can and cannot do
ai-1-what-it-is.summary: Helpful, fast, and not always right.
ai-1-what-it-is.desc: AI tools such as chatbots can write, explain and summarise in seconds. They are useful helpers, but they are not always right.

steps.0: An AI tool predicts likely words. It does not know whether something is true.
steps.1: It can give answers that sound confident but are wrong, or make up facts, quotes and references.
steps.2: It can repeat unfair ideas from the material it learned from.
steps.3: It does not replace your own thinking, your lecturer or your textbook.
steps.4: Treat what it says as a first draft or a starting point, never as the final answer.

ai-1-what-it-is.tip: If an answer really matters, check it against your notes, your textbook or a reliable website.

ai-2-learn-not-cheat.title: Using AI to learn, not to cheat
ai-2-learn-not-cheat.summary: What is a good use, and what breaks the rules.
ai-2-learn-not-cheat.desc: Handing in work an AI wrote and calling it yours is a form of cheating. Used well, AI can help you understand more.

steps.0: Read your module guide and assessment instructions. Each lecturer sets the rules for AI use in their module.
steps.1: If you are not sure whether a tool is allowed, ask your lecturer before you use it.
steps.2: Good uses: ask it to explain an idea in simpler words, quiz you before a test, or suggest how to plan an essay.
steps.3: Risky uses: having it write your assignment, code or answers, and then handing that in as your own work.
steps.4: If AI use is allowed, say how you used it, in the way your lecturer asks.
steps.5: Do the thinking and the writing yourself, so you can explain your work in a test or an oral.

ai-2-learn-not-cheat.tip: A good check: could you explain and defend every line of your work without the AI tool open?

ai-3-privacy.title: Protecting your privacy with AI
ai-3-privacy.summary: What never to type into an AI chat.
ai-3-privacy.desc: What you type into an AI tool may be stored, and used by the company that runs it.

steps.0: Do not type your student number, ID number, passwords, address or bank details into an AI tool.
steps.1: Do not paste in private information about other people, such as their photos or messages.
steps.2: Do not paste in work that belongs to someone else, like a lecturer's test or a classmate's assignment, without permission.
steps.3: Check the tool's privacy settings, and turn off chat history or training on your data if you can.
steps.4: Be careful with free apps that ask for a lot of permissions.

ai-3-privacy.tip: A simple rule: if you would not put it on a public noticeboard, do not put it in an AI chat.

ai-4-check-and-credit.title: Checking and crediting AI output
ai-4-check-and-credit.summary: Verify it, put it in your own words, and be honest.
ai-4-check-and-credit.desc: Before you use anything an AI tool gives you, check it, and be honest about where it came from.

steps.0: Check every fact, date, number and name against a reliable source.
steps.1: Search for any book, article or quote it gives you. AI tools sometimes invent references that do not exist.
steps.2: For code, run it and test it. Make sure you understand each part before you use it.
steps.3: Put ideas in your own words. Copying AI text straight into your work can count as plagiarism.
steps.4: Use the referencing style your department asks for, and follow its rules on mentioning AI.
steps.5: When in doubt, be open about it and ask your lecturer.

ai-4-check-and-credit.tip: You are responsible for everything you hand in, including any mistakes an AI tool made for you.
